arXiv:1408.3902v9 [math.NT] 30 May 2016

Two series expansions for the logarithm of the gamma function involving Stirling numbers and containing only rational
coefficients for certain arguments related to π−1\pi^{-1}

-
Note to the readers of the 9th arXiv version: this is the final arXiv version of this article (first arXiv version was released on 18 August 2014) and it will not be updated in the future. This version differs from the journal version of the paper, which has been published by the Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications (Elsevier), vol. 442, no. 2, pp. 404-434, 2016, DOI 10.1016/J.JMAA.2016.04.032 http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022247X16300701 In particular, the journal version does not contain appendices, but the results contained in both versions are the same (results obtained in appendices of the arXiv version are given in a sketch form in the journal version at the end of Section 2.2, footnotes 30-32 explain how these results were obtained).
Iaroslav V. Blagouchine Email: iaroslav.blagouchine@univ-tln.fr Address: University of Toulon, France. Corresponding author: Corresponding author. Phones: +33–970–46–28–33, +7–953–358–87–23, +7–812–744–76–79.
Abstract

In this paper, two new series for the logarithm of the Γ\Gamma-function are presented and studied. Their polygamma analogs are also obtained and discussed. These series involve the Stirling numbers of the first kind and have the property to contain only rational coefficients for certain arguments related to π−1\pi^{-1}. In particular, for any value of the form ln⁡Γ⁡(12​n±α​π−1)\ln\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}n\pm\alpha\pi^{-1}) and Ψk​(12​n±α​π−1)\Psi_{k}(\frac{1}{2}n\pm\alpha\pi^{-1}), where Ψk\Psi_{k} stands for the kkth polygamma function, α\alpha is positive rational greater than 16​π\frac{1}{6}\pi, nn is integer and kk is non-negative integer, these series have rational terms only. In the specified zones of convergence, derived series converge uniformly at the same rate as ∑(n​lnm​n)−2\sum(n\ln^{m}\!n)^{-2}, where m=1,2,3,…m=1,2,3,\ldots , depending on the order of the polygamma function. Explicit expansions into the series with rational coefficients are given for the most attracting values, such as ln⁡Γ⁡(π−1)\ln\Gamma(\pi^{-1}), ln⁡Γ⁡(2​π−1)\ln\Gamma(2\pi^{-1}), ln⁡Γ⁡(12+π−1)\ln\Gamma(\tfrac{1}{2}+\pi^{-1}), Ψ⁡(π−1)\Psi(\pi^{-1}), Ψ⁡(12+π−1)\Psi(\tfrac{1}{2}+\pi^{-1}) and Ψk​(π−1)\Psi_{k}(\pi^{-1}). Besides, in this article, the reader will also find a number of other series involving Stirling numbers, Gregory’s coefficients (logarithmic numbers, also known as Bernoulli numbers of the second kind), Cauchy numbers and generalized Bernoulli numbers. Finally, several estimations and full asymptotics for Gregory’s coefficients, for Cauchy numbers, for certain generalized Bernoulli numbers and for certain sums with the Stirling numbers are obtained. In particular, these include sharp bounds for Gregory’s coefficients and for the Cauchy numbers of the second kind.

Keywords:
Gamma function, Digamma function, Psi function, Polygamma functions, Series expansions, Stirling numbers, Factorial coefficients, Rational coefficients, Gregory’s coefficients, Logarithmic numbers, Cauchy numbers, Generalized Bernoulli numbers, Bernoulli numbers of higher order, Bounds, Asymptotic formulæ, Approximations, Pi, Exotic arguments.

I Introduction

I.1 Motivation of the study

Numerous are expansions of the logarithm of the Γ\Gamma–function and of polygamma functions into various series. For instance

which are respectively known as Stirling’s series11 1 This series expansion is one of the oldest and was known to Gauss [51, p. 33], Euler [46, part II, Chapter VI, § 159, p. 466], Stirling [146, p. 135] and De Moivre [148], who originated it. I], [42]. Usually, coefficients of such expansions are either highly transcendental, or seriously suspected to be so. Expansions into the series with rational coefficients are much less investigated, and especially for the gamma and polygamma functions of “exotic” arguments, such as, for example, π−1\pi^{-1}, logarithms or complex values.

In one of our preceding works, in exercises no 39–49 [13, Sect. 4], we have evaluated several curious integrals containing inverse circular and hyperbolic functions, which led to the gamma and polygamma functions at rational multiple of π−1\pi^{-1}. It appears that some of these integrals are particularly suitable for power series expansions. In this paper, we derive two series expansions for the logarithm of the Γ\Gamma–function, as well as their respective analogs for the polygamma functions, by making use of such a kind of integrals. These expansions are not simple and cannot be explicitly written in powers of zz up to a given order, but they contain rational coefficients for any argument of the form z=12​n±α​π−1z=\frac{1}{2}n\pm\alpha\pi^{-1}, where α\alpha is positive rational greater than 16​π\frac{1}{6}\pi and nn is integer, and therefore, may be of interest in certain situations. As examples, we provide explicit expansions into the series with rational coefficients for ln⁡Γ⁡(π−1)\ln\Gamma(\pi^{-1}), ln⁡Γ⁡(2​π−1)\ln\Gamma(2\pi^{-1}), ln⁡Γ⁡(12+π−1)\ln\Gamma(\tfrac{1}{2}+\pi^{-1}), Ψ⁡(π−1)\Psi(\pi^{-1}), Ψ⁡(12+π−1)\Psi(\tfrac{1}{2}+\pi^{-1}) and Ψk​(π−1)\Psi_{k}(\pi^{-1}). Coefficients of discovered expansions involve the Stirling numbers of the first kind, which often appear in combinatorics, as well as in various “exotic” series expansions, such as, for example

which is probably due to Arthur Cayley who gave it in 1859,99 9 Cayley [31] did not present the formula in the same form as we did, he only gave first six coefficients for formula (20) from p. 20. He noticed that the law for the formation of these coefficients “is a very complicated one” and that they are related in some way to Stirling numbers. The exact relationship between series (11) and Stirling’s polynomials (and, hence, Stirling numbers) was established later by Niels Nielsen [110, p. 76], [111, p. 36. eq. (8)], see also [8, vol. III, p. 257, eqs. 19.7(58)–19.7(63)]. By the way, coefficients of this particular series are also strongly correlated with Cauchy numbers of the second kind, see (19), (21), footnote 22 and (126). or a very similar expansion converging to Euler’s constant

γ=12+124+172+192880+3800+863362 880+275169 344+33 95329 030 400+…=∑n=1∞(−1)n−1n⋅1n!∑l=1nS1​(n,l)l+1\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\gamma&\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{24}+\frac{1}{72}+\frac{19}{2880}+\frac{3}{800}+\frac{863}{362\,880}+\frac{275}{169\,344}+\frac{33\,953}{29\,030\,400}+\ldots\\[14.22636pt] &\displaystyle=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{\,(-1)^{n-1}\,}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{\,n!\,}\!\sum_{l=1}^{n}\!\frac{\,S_{1}(n,l)\,}{l+1}\end{array} (12)

which was given by Lorenzo Mascheroni in 1790 [98, p. 23] and was subsequently rediscovered several times (in particular, by Ernst Schröder in 1879 [134, p. 115, Eq. (25a)], by Niels E. Nørlund in 1923 [112, p. 244], by Jan C. Kluyver in 1924 [78], by Charles Jordan in 1929 [74, p. 148], by Kenter in 1999 [77], by Victor Kowalenko in 2008 [83], [82]).1010 10 The series itself was given by Gregorio Fontana, who, however, failed to find a constant to which it converges (he only proved that it should be lesser than 1). Mascheroni identified this Fontana’s constant and showed that it equals Euler’s constant [98, pp. 21–23]. Taking into account that both Fontana and Mascheroni did practically the equal work, series (12) is called throughout the paper Fontana–Mascheroni’s series. Coefficients of this series are usually witten in terms of Gregory’s coefficients, see (18), (21) and footnote 21. At large nn and moderate values of argument zz, discovered series converge approximately at the same rate as ∑(n​lnm​n)−2\sum\,(n\ln^{m}n)^{-2}\,, where m=1m=1 for ln⁡Γ⁡(z)\ln\Gamma(z) and Ψ⁡(z)\Psi(z), m=2m=2 for Ψ1​(z)\Psi_{1}(z) and Ψ2​(z)\Psi_{2}(z), m=3m=3 for Ψ3​(z)\Psi_{3}(z) and Ψ4​(z)\Psi_{4}(z), etc. At the same time, first partial sums of the series may behave quite irregularly, and the sign of its general term changes in a complex pattern. However, in all cases, including small and moderate values of nn, the absolute value of the nnth general term remains bounded by α​n−2\alpha n^{-2}, where α\alpha does not depend on nn. Finally, in the manuscript, we also obtain a number of other series expansions containing Stirling numbers, Gregory’s coefficients (logarithmic numbers, also known as Bernoulli numbers of the second kind), Cauchy numbers, ordinary and generalized Bernoulli numbers, binomial coefficients and harmonic numbers, as well as provide the convergence analysis for some of them.

II Stirling numbers and their role in various expansions

II.1 General information in brief

Stirling numbers were introduced by the Scottish mathematician James Stirling in his famous treatise [146, pp. 1–11], and were subsequently rediscovered in various forms by numerous authors, including Christian Kramp, Pierre–Simon Laplace, Andreas von Ettingshausen, Ludwig Schläffli, Oskar Schlömilch, Paul Appel, Arthur Cayley, George Boole, James Glaisher, Leonard Carlitz and many others [68], [84], [94, Book I, part I], [45], [128], [129], [130], [131, pp. 186–187], [132, vol. II, pp. 23–31], [5], [30], [31], [32], [16], [55], [26, p. 129], [110, pp. 67–78], [76, p. 1], [59], [80].1515 15 Although it is largely accepted that these numbers were introduced by James Stirling in his famous treatise [146] published in 1730, Donald E. Knuth [80, p. 416] rightly remarks that these numbers may be much older. In particular, the above–mentioned writer found them in an old unpublished manuscript of Thomas Harriot, dating about 1600. Traditionally, Stirling numbers are devided in two different “kinds”: Stirling numbers of the first kind and those of the second kind, albeit there really is only one “kind” of Stirling numbers [see the remark after Eq. (16)].1616 16 Within the framework of our study we are not concerned with the Stirling numbers of the second kind; we, therefore, will not treat them here. By the way, it is interesting that Stirling himself, first, introduced numbers of the second kind [146, p. 8], and then, those of the first kind [146, p. 11]. The Stirling numbers of the first kind appear in numerous occasions in combinatorics, in calculus of finite differences, in numerical analysis, in number theory and even in calculus of variations. In combinatorics, Stirling numbers of the first kind, denoted |S1​(n,l)||S_{1}(n,l)|, are defined as the number of ways to arrange nn objects into ll cycles or cyclic arrangements (|S1​(n,l)||S_{1}(n,l)| is often verbalized “nn cycle ll”). These numbers are also called unsigned (or signless) Stirling numbers, as opposed to S1​(n,l)S_{1}(n,l), which are called signed Stirling numbers and which are related to the former as S1​(n,l)=(−1)n±l​|S1​(n,l)|S_{1}(n,l)=(-1)^{n\pm l}|S_{1}(n,l)|. In the analysis and related disciplines, the unsigned/signed Stirling numbers of the first kind are usually defined as the coefficients in the expansion of rising/falling factorial

{∏k=0n−1(z+k)=(z)n=Γ⁡(z+n)Γ⁡(z)=∑l=1n|S1​(n,l)|⋅zl∏k=0n−1(z−k)=(z−n+1)n=Γ⁡(z+1)Γ⁡(z+1−n)=∑l=1nS1​(n,l)⋅zl\begin{cases}\displaystyle\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(z+k)\,=\,(z)_{n}\,=\,\frac{\Gamma(z+n)}{\Gamma(z)}\,=\,\sum_{l=1}^{n}|S_{1}(n,l)|\cdot z^{l}\\[14.22636pt] \displaystyle\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(z-k)\,=\,(z-n+1)_{n}\,=\frac{\Gamma(z+1)}{\Gamma(z+1-n)}\,=\,\sum_{l=1}^{n}S_{1}(n,l)\cdot z^{l}\end{cases} (14)

where z∈ℂz\in\mathbbm{C} and n⩾1n\geqslant 1. Stirling numbers of the first kind are also often introduced via their generating functions

{∑n=l∞|S1​(n,l)|n!zn=(−1)llnl⁡(1−z)l!,l=0,1,2,…∑n=l∞S1​(n,l)n!zn=lnl⁡(1+z)l!,l=0,1,2,…\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{n=l}^{\infty}\!\frac{|S_{1}(n,l)|}{n!}z^{n}=\,(-1)^{l}\frac{\ln^{l}(1-z)}{l!}\,,\qquad&l=0,1,2,\ldots\\[14.22636pt] \displaystyle\sum_{n=l}^{\infty}\!\frac{S_{1}(n,l)}{n!}z^{n}=\,\frac{\ln^{l}(1+z)}{l!}\,,\qquad&l=0,1,2,\ldots\end{cases} (15)

both series on the left being uniformly and absolutely convergent on the disk |z|<1|z|<1.1717 17 Remark that formally, in (15), the summation may be started not only from n=ln=l, but from any nn in the range [0,l−1][0,l-1], because S1​(n,l)=0S_{1}(n,l)=0 for such nn. Signed Stirling numbers of the first kind may be calculated explicitly via the following formula

S1​(n,l)={(2​n−l)!(l−1)!∑k=0n−l1(n+k)​(n−l−k)!​(n−l+k)!∑r=0k(−1)r​rn−l+kr!​(k−r)!,l∈[1,n]1,n=0,l=00,otherwiseS_{1}(n,l)\,=\,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{(2n-l)!}{(l-1)!}\sum_{k=0}^{n-l}\frac{1}{(n+k)(n-l-k)!(n-l+k)!}\sum_{r=0}^{k}\frac{(-1)^{r}r^{n-l+k}}{r!(k-r)!}\,,\quad&l\in[1,n]\\[8.53581pt] 1\,,&n=0\,,\,l=0\\[2.84526pt] 0\,,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (16)

where S1​(0,0)=1\,S_{1}(0,0)=1\, by convention.1818 18 In the above, we always supposed that nn and ll are nonnegative, although, this, strictly speaking, is not necessary. In fact, for negative arguments nn and ll, Stirling numbers of the first kind reduce to those of the second kind and vice–versa, see e.g. [80, p. 412], [60, p. 116], [63, p. 60 et seq.]. From the above definitions, it is visible that numbers S1​(n,l)S_{1}(n,l) are necessarily integers: S1​(1,1)=+1S_{1}(1,1)=+1, S1​(2,1)=−1S_{1}(2,1)=-1, S1​(2,2)=+1S_{1}(2,2)=+1, S1​(3,1)=+2S_{1}(3,1)=+2, S1​(3,2)=−3S_{1}(3,2)=-3, S1​(3,3)=+1S_{1}(3,3)=+1, … , S1​(8,5)=−1 960S_{1}(8,5)=-1\,960, … , S1​(9,3)=+118 124S_{1}(9,3)=+118\,124, etc.

Stirling numbers of the first kind were studied in a large number of works and have many various properties which we cannot describe in a small article. These numbers are of great utility, especially, for the summation of series, the fact which was noticed primarily by Stirling in his marvellous treatise [146] and which was later emphasized by numerous writers. In particular, Charles Jordan, who worked a lot on Stirling numbers, see e.g. [76], [74], [75], remarked that these numbers may be even more important than Bernoulli numbers. In what follows we give only a small amount of the information necessary for the understanding of the rest of our work. Readers interested in a more deep study of these numbers are kindly invited to refer to the above–cited historical references, as well as to the following specialized literature: [76, Chapt. IV], [74], [75], [109], [110, pp. 67–78], [111], [155], [61, Sect. 6.1], [80, pp. 410–422], [38, Chapt. V], [43], [117, Chapt. 4, § 3, no 196–210], [63, p. 60 et seq.], [108], [122, p. 70 et seq.], [142, vol. 1], [11], [34, Chapt. 8], [1, no 24.1.3, p. 824], [81, Sect. 21.5-1, p. 824], [8, vol. III, § 19.7], [112], [145], [39, pp. 91–94], [159, pp. 2862–2865], [6, Chapt. 2], [101], [58], [60], [59], [157], [26], [28], [114, p. 642], [126], [54], [162], [103], [10], [161], [147], [69], [23], [22], [72], [2], [152], [62], [96], [136], [137], [127], [123], [124], [65], [90]. Note that many writers discovered these numbers independently, without realizing that they deal with the Stirling numbers. For this reason, in many sources, these numbers may appear under different names, different notations and even slightly different definitions. Actually, only in the beginning of the XXth century, the name “Stirling numbers” appeared in mathematical literature (mainly, thanks to Thorvald N. Thiele and Niels Nielsen [109], [155], [80, p. 416]). Other names for these numbers include: factorial coefficients, faculty’s coefficients (Facultätencoefficienten, coefficients de la faculté analytique), differences of zero and even differential coefficients of nothing. The Stirling numbers are also closely connected to the generalized Bernoulli numbers Bn(s)B^{(s)}_{n}, also known as Bernoulli numbers of higher order, see e.g. [26, p. 129], [58, p. 449], [60, p. 116], [8, vol. III, § 19.7], [165], [20], [19]; many of their properties may be, therefore, deduced from those of Bn(s)B^{(s)}_{n}. As concerns notations, there exist more than 50 notations for them, see e.g. [60], [76, pp. vii–viii, 142, 168], [80, pp. 410–422], [61, Sect. 6.1], and we do not insist on our particular notation, which may seem for certain not properly chosen. Lastly, we remark that there also are several slightly different definitions of the Stirling numbers of the first kind; our definitions (14)–(16) agree with those adopted by Jordan [76, Chapt. IV], [74], [75], Riordan [122, p. 70 et seq.], Mitrinović [101], Abramowitz & Stegun [1, no 24.1.3, p. 824] and many others.1919 19 Modern CAS, such as Maple or Mathematica, also share these definitions; in particular Stirling1(n,l) in the former and StirlingS1[n,l] in the latter correspond to our S1​(n,l)S_{1}(n,l). A quick analysis of several alternative definitions may be found in [60], [59], [76, pp. vii–viii and Chapt. IV], [80, pp. 410–422].

II.2 MacLaurin series expansions of certain composite functions and some other series with Stirling numbers

Let now focus our attention on expansions (15). An appropriate use of these series provides numerous fascinating formulæ, and especially, the series expansions of the MacLaurin–Taylor type for the composite functions involving logarithms and inverse trigonometric and hyperbolic functions. The technique is based of the summation over ll of (15), on the fact that S1​(n,l)S_{1}(n,l) vanishes for l∉[1,n]l\notin[1,n] and on the interchanging the order of summation2020 20 Series in question being absolutely convergent.. For example, the trivial summation of the right part of (15b) over l∈[1,∞)l\in[1,\infty), yields

∑l=1∞lnl⁡(1+z)l!=eln⁡(z+1)−1=z\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}\frac{\ln^{l}(1+z)}{l!}=e^{\ln(z+1)}-1=z

since the sum in the left–hand side is simply the MacLaurin series of eln⁡(z+1)\,e^{\ln(z+1)} without the first term. At the same time, the summation of the left part of (15b) results in

∑l=1∞∑n=l∞S1​(n,l)n!​zn=∑l=1∞∑n=1∞S1​(n,l)n!​zn=∑n=1∞znn!​∑l=1nS1​(n,l)⏟δn,1=z\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}\sum_{n=l}^{\infty}\!\frac{S_{1}(n,l)}{n!}z^{n}=\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{S_{1}(n,l)}{n!}z^{n}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{z^{n}}{n!}\underbrace{\sum_{l=1}^{n}S_{1}(n,l)}_{\delta_{n,1}}=z

where the last sum may be truncated at l=nl=n thanks to (16) and equals 1 if n=1n=1 and 0 otherwise. Let now consider more complicated cases. Write in (15b) 2​l2l for ll, and then, sum the result with respect to ll from l=1l=1 to l=∞l=\infty. This gives

chln⁡(1+z)= 1+∑n=1∞znn!⋅∑l=1⌊12​n⌋S1​(n,2​l)=1+12​∑n=2∞(−1)n​zn,|z|<1\mathop{\rm ch}\nolimits\ln(1+z)\,=\,1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{z^{n}}{n!}\cdot\!\!\sum_{l=1}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!S_{1}(n,2l)=1+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}z^{n}\,,\qquad|z|<1 (17)

By the same line of reasoning, if we divide the right–hand side of (15b) by l+1l+1 and sum it over l∈[1,∞)l\in[1,\infty), then we get

∑l=1∞1l+1⋅lnl⁡(1+z)l!=1ln⁡(1+z)​∑l=1∞lnl+1⁡(1+z)(l+1)!=1ln⁡(1+z)​[eln⁡(1+z)−ln⁡(1+z)−1]=zln⁡(1+z)−1\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{l+1}\cdot\frac{\ln^{l}(1+z)}{l!}\,=\,\frac{1}{\ln(1+z)}\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{\ln^{l+1}(1+z)}{(l+1)!}\\[14.22636pt] \displaystyle\qquad\,=\,\frac{1}{\ln(1+z)}\left[e^{\ln(1+z)}-\ln(1+z)-1\right]\,=\,\frac{z}{\ln(1+z)}-1\end{array}

Applying the same operation to the left–hand side of (15b) and comparing both sides yields

zln⁡(1+z)= 1+∑n=1∞zn⋅1n!​∑l=1nS1​(n,l)l+1⏟Gn= 1+∑n=1∞Gn​zn,|z|<1,\frac{z}{\ln(1+z)}\,=\,1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}z^{n}\!\cdot\!\underbrace{\frac{1}{n!}\!\sum_{l=1}^{n}\frac{S_{1}(n,l)}{l+1}}_{G_{n}}\,=\,1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}G_{n}\,z^{n}\,,\quad\qquad|z|<1\,, (18)

the equality, which is more known as the generating equation for the Gregory’s coefficients GnG_{n} (in particular, G1=+12G_{1}=+\frac{1}{2}, G2=−112G_{2}=-\frac{1}{12}, G3=+124G_{3}=+\frac{1}{24}, G4=−19720G_{4}=-\frac{19}{720}, G5=+3160G_{5}=+\frac{3}{160}, G6=−86360 480G_{6}=-\frac{863}{60\,480}, …).2121 21 Coefficients Gn=1n!​∑l=1nS1​(n,l)l+1=1n!​∫01(x−n+1)n​𝑑x=−Bn(n−1)(n−1)​n!=C1,nn!\,G_{n}=\frac{1}{n!}\sum\limits_{l=1}^{n}\frac{S_{1}(n,l)}{l+1}=\frac{1}{n!}\int\limits_{0}^{1}(x-n+1)_{n}\,dx=-\frac{B_{n}^{(n-1)}}{(n-1)\,n!}=\frac{C_{1,n}}{n!}\, are also called (reciprocal) logarithmic numbers, Bernoulli numbers of the second kind, normalized generalized Bernoulli numbers Bn(n−1)B_{n}^{(n-1)}, Cauchy numbers and normalized Cauchy numbers of the first kind C1,nC_{1,n}. They were introduced by James Gregory in 1670 in the context of area’s interpolation formula (which is known nowdays as Gregory’s interpolation formula) and were subsequently rediscovered in various contexts by many famous mathematicians, including Gregorio Fontana, Lorenzo Mascheroni , Pierre–Simon Laplace, Augustin–Louis Cauchy, Jacques Binet, Ernst Schröder, Oskar Schlömilch, Charles Hermite, Jan C. The use of the same and of similar techniques allows to readily derive expressions for the coefficients of the MacLaurin series for even more complicated functions. Derived expansions coincide with the corresponding MacLaurin series, converge everywhere where expanded functions are analytic2424 24 The radius of convergence of such series rr is conditioned by the singularities of expanded functions. For instance, ln⁡[1+ln⁡(1+z)]\ln\!\big[1+\ln(1+z)\big] is analytic on the entire complex zz–plane except points at which 1+z=01+z=0 and 1+ln⁡(1+z)=01+\ln(1+z)=0, which are both branch points. From the former we conclude that the radius of convergence cannot be greater than 1, and from the latter, it follows that it cannot exceed 1−e−11-e^{-1} which is even lesser than 1. Hence r=1−e−1≈0.63r=1-e^{-1}\approx 0.63 and contain rational coefficients only. The main advantage of this technique is that we do not need to “mechanically” compute the nnth derivative of the composite function at z=0z=0, which often may be a very laborious task.2525 25 Some other power series expansions involving Stirling numbers are also given in works of Wilf [162], Kruchinin [86], [88], [87] and Rza̧dkowski [125]. Moreover, series expansions of certain composite functions, not necessarily containing Stirling numbers, may be found in [79, Chapt. VI], [150, p. 20 & 63], [64] and [119, vol. I] (in the third reference, the author also provides a list of related references),2626 26 Since these expansions are not particularly difficult to obtain and also may be derived by other techniques, it is possible that some of them could appear in earlier works. The same remark also concerns formulæ (44)–(55). For instance, formula (48) may be found in other sources as well, see e.g. [83, p. 431, Eq. (76)], [4, p. 128, Eq. (7.3.11)], [167, p. 4006] (the same series also appears in [36, p. 14, Eq. (2.39)], but the result is incorrect). Series (51) is also known, see e.g. [166, p. 2952, Eq. (1.3)], [36, p. 20, Eq. (3.6)], [25, p. 307, Eq. for F0​(2)F_{0}(2)].

Generating equations for Stirling numbers of the first kind may be also successfully used for the derivation of more complicated and quite unexpected results. For instance, it is known that

ζ(k+1)=∑n=k∞|S1​(n,k)|n⋅n!,k=1,2,3,…\zeta(k+1)\,=\,\sum_{n=k}^{\infty}\frac{|S_{1}(n,k)|}{n\cdot n!}\,,\qquad\quad k=1,2,3,\ldots (40)

see e.g. Jordan’s book [76, pp. 166, 194–195].2727 27 Jordan derives this formula and remarks that particular cases of it were certainly known to Stirling [146] (see also [109, p. 302, Eq. (36bis)], [155, p. 10], and compare it to formulæ from [146, p. 11]). This result was recently rediscovered by several modern writers, e.g. by Shen [136] and Sato [127]; however, their proofs are exceedingly long. Using (15) the whole procedure takes only a few lines:

∑n=k∞|S1​(n,k)|n⋅n!=∑n=k∞|S1​(n,k)|n!​∫01xn−1​dx⏟1/n=∫01∑n=k∞|S1​(n,k)|n!​xn⏟see (15)​d​xx=(−1)kk!​∫01lnk⁡(1−x)x​𝑑x=(−1)kk!​∫0∞(−t)ket​(1−e−t)​dt=1Γ⁡(k+1)​∫0∞tket−1​dt=ζ⁡(k+1)\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\sum_{n=k}^{\infty}\frac{|S_{1}(n,k)|}{n\cdot n!}\,=\,\sum_{n=k}^{\infty}\frac{|S_{1}(n,k)|}{n!}\!\underbrace{\int\limits_{0}^{1}\!x^{n-1}dx}_{1/n}\,=\int\limits_{0}^{1}\!\underbrace{\sum_{n=k}^{\infty}\frac{|S_{1}(n,k)|}{n!}\,x^{n}}_{\text{see \eqref{h37qp2b237ds}}}\frac{dx}{x}\,=\,\frac{(-1)^{k}}{k!}\int\limits_{0}^{1}\!\frac{\ln^{k}(1-x)}{x}\,dx\\[22.76219pt] \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\;\,=\,\frac{(-1)^{k}}{k!}\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\!\frac{(-t)^{k}}{\,e^{t}\big(1-e^{-t}\big)\,}\,dt\,=\,\frac{1}{\Gamma(k+1)}\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\!\frac{t^{k}}{\,e^{t}-1\,}\,dt\,=\,\zeta(k+1)\end{array} (41)

where in last integrals we made a change of variable x=1−e−t\,x=1-e^{-t}. The above formula may be readily generalized to

ζ(k+1,v)=∑n=k∞|S1​(n,k)|n⋅(v)n,k=1,2,3,…,Rev>0.\zeta(k+1,v)\,=\,\sum_{n=k}^{\infty}\frac{|S_{1}(n,k)|}{n\cdot(v)_{n}}\,,\qquad\quad k=1,2,3,\ldots\,,\qquad\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits v>0\,. (42)

where at large nn

|S1​(n,k)|n⋅(v)n∼Γ⁡(v)(k−1)!⋅lnk−1⁡nnv+1,n→∞,\frac{|S_{1}(n,k)|}{n\cdot(v)_{n}}\,\sim\,\frac{\Gamma(v)}{\,(k-1)!\,}\cdot\frac{\ln^{k-1}\!n}{n^{v+1}}\,,\qquad\qquad n\to\infty\,, (43)

in virtue of (13) and a known asymptotics for the Stirling numbers [75, p. 261], [76, p. 161], [1, no 24.1.3, p. 824], [161, p. 348, Eq. (8)]. Moreover, by a slight modification of the above technique, we may also obtain the following results:

∑n=1∞(−1)n−1n⋅1n!∑l=1nf(l)S1(n,l)=∑l=1∞(−1)l+1f(l)ζ(l+1),∑n=1∞(−1)n−1​Hnn⋅1n!∑l=1nf(l)S1(n,l)=∑l=1∞(−1)l+1(l+1)f(l)ζ(l+2),\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{\,(-1)^{n-1}\,}{\,n\,}\cdot\frac{1}{\,n!\,}\sum_{l=1}^{n}f(l)\,S_{1}(n,l)\,=\,\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{l+1}f(l)\zeta(l+1)\,,\\[17.07164pt] \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{\,(-1)^{n-1}H_{n}\,}{\,n\,}\cdot\frac{1}{\,n!\,}\sum_{l=1}^{n}f(l)\,S_{1}(n,l)\,=\,\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{l+1}(l+1)f(l)\zeta(l+2)\,,\end{array} (44)

where f⁡(l)f(l) is an arbitrary function ensuring the convergence and HnH_{n} is the nnth harmonic number;

∑n=1∞(−1)n−1n⋅1n!∑l=1nS1​(n,l)l+k=∑l=2∞(−1)l⋅ζ⁡(l)l+k−1= 1k−1−ln⁡2​πk+γ2+∑l=1⌊12​(k−1)⌋(−1)l(k−12​l−1)(2​l)!⋅ζ′​(2​l)l⋅(2​π)2​l+∑l=1⌊12​k⌋−1(−1)l(k−12​l)(2​l)!⋅ζ⁡(2​l+1)2⋅(2​π)2​l\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{\,(-1)^{n-1}\,}{\,n\,}\cdot\,\frac{1}{\,n!\,}\sum_{l=1}^{n}\!\frac{\,S_{1}(n,l)\,}{l+k}\,=\sum_{l=2}^{\infty}\!\frac{(-1)^{l}\!\cdot\zeta(l)}{\,l+k-1\,}\,=\,\frac{\,1\,}{\,k-1\,}-\frac{\,\ln 2\pi\,}{k}+\frac{\,\gamma\,}{2}\\[17.07164pt] \displaystyle\qquad+\!\!\!\!\sum_{l=1}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}(k-1)\rfloor}\!\!\!\!(-1)^{l}\binom{k-1}{2l-1}\frac{\,(2l)!\cdot\zeta^{\prime}(2l)\,}{l\cdot(2\pi)^{2l}}+\!\!\sum_{l=1}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}k\rfloor-1}\!\!(-1)^{l}\binom{k-1}{2l}\frac{\,(2l)!\cdot\zeta(2l+1)\,}{2\cdot(2\pi)^{2l}}\end{array} (45)

where k=2,3,4,…k=2,3,4,\,\ldots  and where the series on the left converges as ∑n−2​ln−k−1​n\,\sum n^{-2}\ln^{-k-1}\!n\,; for k=1,2,3,…k=1,2,3,\ldots

∑n=1∞(−1)n−1n+k⋅1n!∑l=1nS1​(n,l)l+1=∑n=1∞|Gn|n+k=1k+∑m=1k(−1)m(km)ln(m+1)\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{\,(-1)^{n-1}\,}{\,n+k\,}\cdot\frac{1}{\,n!\,}\sum_{l=1}^{n}\frac{\,S_{1}(n,l)\,}{l+1}\,=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{\big|\,G_{n}\big|}{\,n+k\,}\,=\,\frac{1}{k}+\sum_{m=1}^{k}(-1)^{m}\binom{k}{m}\ln(m+1)
=1k+Δk​ln⁡(x)|x=1\displaystyle\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\;\,\,=\,\frac{1}{k}+\Big.\Delta^{k}\ln(x)\Big|_{x=1}\, (46)
∑n=1∞(−1)n−1n⋅1n!∑l=1nS1​(n,l)l+1=∑n=1∞|Gn|n=γ\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{\,(-1)^{n-1}\,}{\,n\,}\cdot\frac{1}{\,n!\,}\sum_{l=1}^{n}\frac{\,S_{1}(n,l)\,}{l+1}\,=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\big|\,G_{n}\big|}{n}\,=\,\gamma (47)
∑n=2∞(−1)n−1n−1⋅1n!∑l=1nS1​(n,l)l+1=∑n=2∞|Gn|n−1=−12+ln⁡2​π2−γ2\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\!\frac{\,(-1)^{n-1}\,}{\,n-1\,}\cdot\frac{1}{\,n!\,}\sum_{l=1}^{n}\frac{\,S_{1}(n,l)\,}{l+1}\,=\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\!\frac{\big|\,G_{n}\big|}{\,n-1\,}\,=\,-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\ln 2\pi}{2}-\frac{\gamma}{2}\ (48)
∑n=3∞(−1)n−1n−2⋅1n!∑l=1nS1​(n,l)l+1=∑n=3∞|Gn|n−2=−18+ln⁡2​π12−ζ′​(2) 2​π2\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{n=3}^{\infty}\!\frac{\,(-1)^{n-1}\,}{\,n-2\,}\cdot\frac{1}{\,n!\,}\sum_{l=1}^{n}\frac{\,S_{1}(n,l)\,}{l+1}\,=\sum_{n=3}^{\infty}\!\frac{\big|\,G_{n}\big|}{\,n-2\,}\,=\,-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{\ln 2\pi}{12}-\frac{\zeta^{\prime}(2)}{\,2\pi^{2}} (49)

where Δk\Delta^{k} is the kkth finite difference, see e.g. [156, p. 270, Eq. (14.17)], and where all series on the left converges as ∑(n​ln⁡n)−2\,\sum(n\ln n)^{-2}\,;

∑n=1∞(−1)n−1​Hnn⋅1n!∑l=1nS1​(n,l)l+1=∑n=1∞|Gn|⋅Hnn=π26−1\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{\,(-1)^{n-1}H_{n}\,}{\,n\,}\cdot\frac{1}{\,n!\,}\sum_{l=1}^{n}\frac{\,S_{1}(n,l)\,}{l+1}\,=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{\,\big|\,G_{n}\big|\cdot H_{n}\,}{\,n\,}\!\,=\,\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}-1 (51)
∑n=1∞(−1)n−1​Hnn⋅1n!∑l=1nS1​(n,l)(l+1)​(l+2)=π212−γ\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{\,(-1)^{n-1}H_{n}\,}{\,n\,}\cdot\frac{1}{\,n!\,}\sum_{l=1}^{n}\frac{\,S_{1}(n,l)\,}{\,(l+1)(l+2)\,}\,=\,\frac{\pi^{2}}{12}-\gamma (52)
∑n=1∞(−1)n−1​Hnn⋅1n!∑l=1nS1​(n,l)(l+1)​(l+3)=π218+12ln2π−γ2−\displaystyle\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{\,(-1)^{n-1}H_{n}\,}{\,n\,}\cdot\frac{1}{\,n!\,}\sum_{l=1}^{n}\frac{\,S_{1}(n,l)\,}{\,(l+1)(l+3)\,}\,=\,\frac{\pi^{2}}{18}+\frac{1}{2}\ln 2\pi-\frac{\gamma}{2}-1\! (53)

which all converge as ∑n−2​ln−1​n\sum n^{-2}\ln^{-1}\!n, and even this beautiful alternating series

∑n=1∞ 1n⋅1n!∑l=1nS1​(n,l)l+1=∑n=1∞Gnn=Ei(ln2)−γ=li(2)−γ,\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{\,1\,}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{\,n!\,}\!\sum_{l=1}^{n}\!\frac{\,S_{1}(n,l)\,}{l+1}\,=\sum\limits_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{\,G_{n}\,}{n}\,=\,\mathop{\rm Ei}\nolimits(\ln 2)-\gamma\,=\,\mathop{\rm li}\nolimits(2)-\gamma\,, (54)

where Ei(⋅)\mathop{\rm Ei}\nolimits(\cdot) and li(⋅)\mathop{\rm li}\nolimits(\cdot) denote exponential integral and logarithmic integral functions respectively.2828 28 Numbers GnG_{n} are strictly alternating: Gn=(−1)n−1​|Gn|G_{n}=(-1)^{n-1}\big|G_{n}\big|\,. The left side of (54) is, therefore, the alternating variant of Fontana–Mascheroni’s series (12), (47), and from various points of view the constant li(2)−γ= 0.4679481152​…\,\mathop{\rm li}\nolimits(2)-\gamma\,=\,0.4679481152\ldots may be regarded as the alternating Euler’s constant, by analogy to ln⁡4π\,\ln\frac{4}{\pi}\,, which was earlier proposed as such by Jonathan Sondow in [138]. Finally, Stirling numbers of the first kind may also appear in the evaluation of certain integrals, which, at first sight, have nothing to do with Stirling numbers. For instance, if kk is positive integer and Res>k−1\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits{s}>k-1, then

∫01lns⁡(1−x)xk​𝑑x=(−1)s⋅Γ⁡(s+1)(k−1)!⋅{ζ(s+1),k=1ζ(s),k=2ζ(s−1)+ζ(s),k=3ζ(s−2)+3ζ(s−1)+2ζ(s),k=4∑r=1k−1S1(k−1,r)∑m=0r(rm)⋅(k−2)r−m⋅ζ(s+1−m),k⩾3\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\int\limits_{0}^{1}\!\frac{\,\ln^{s}(1-x)\,}{x^{k}}\,dx\,=\,\frac{\,(-1)^{s}\!\cdot\Gamma(s+1)\,}{(k-1)!}\cdot\begin{cases}\,\zeta(s+1)\,,\quad&k=1\\[5.69054pt] \,\zeta(s)\,,\quad&k=2\\[4.55244pt] \,\zeta(s-1)+\zeta(s)\,,\quad&k=3\\[4.55244pt] \,\zeta(s-2)+3\zeta(s-1)+2\zeta(s)\,,\quad&k=4\\[4.55244pt] \displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{k-1}S_{1}(k-1,r)\!\sum_{m=0}^{r}\!\binom{r}{m}\!\cdot(k-2)^{r-m}\cdot\zeta(s+1-m)\,,\quad&k\geqslant 3\end{cases}\end{array} (55)

The proofs of some of these results being quite long, we placed them in A.

II.3 An inspiring example for the derivation of the series for ln⁡Γ⁡(z)\ln\Gamma(z)

Let now consider the example which was originally our inspiration for this work. In exercise no 39-b in [13, Sect. 4] we established that

∫0 1arc​tg⁡arcth⁡xx​𝑑x=π⁡{ln⁡Γ⁡(1π)−ln⁡Γ⁡(12+1π)−12​ln​π}= 1.025760510​…\int\limits_{0}^{\,1}\!\frac{\,\mathop{\mathrm{arc\,tg}}\nolimits\mathop{\rm arcth}\nolimits{x}\,}{x}\,dx=\,\pi\left\{\ln\Gamma\!\left(\!\dfrac{1}{\,\pi\,}\!\right)-\ln\Gamma\!\left(\!\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{\,\pi\,}\!\right)-\frac{1}{2}\ln\pi\right\}=\,1.025760510\ldots (56)

The arctangent of the hyperbolic arctangent is analytic in the whole disk |x|<1|x|<1, and therefore, can be expanded into the MacLaurin series.2929 29 Function arc​tg⁡arcth⁡x\mathop{\mathrm{arc\,tg}}\nolimits\mathop{\rm arcth}\nolimits x has branch points at x=±1x=\pm 1 and x=±itg1≈±1.56ix=\pm i\mathop{\mathrm{tg}}\nolimits 1\approx\pm 1.56i. The coefficients of such an expansion require a careful watching, the law for their formation being difficult to derive by inductive or semi–inductive methods. So we resort again to the method employing Stirling numbers:

arc​tg⁡arcth⁡x=∑l=0∞(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅arcth2​l+1x(2​l+1)!=∑n=1∞xn⋅∑k=1n(n−1k−1)​2kk!⋅∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l⋅(2​l)!⋅S1​(k,2​l+1)22​l+1=∑n=0∞x2​n+1⋅∑k=12​n+1(2​nk−1)​2kk!⋅∑l=0n(−1)l⋅(2​l)!⋅S1​(k,2​l+1)22​l+1⏟An=x+115​x5+ 145​x7+ 642835​x9+ 714725​x11+ 5209405 405​x13+2 203 328212 837 625​x15+…,|x|<1,\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle\mathop{\mathrm{arc\,tg}}\nolimits\mathop{\rm arcth}\nolimits{x}\,=\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{l}(2l)!\cdot\frac{\mathop{\rm arcth}\nolimits^{2l+1}\!x}{(2l+1)!}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x^{n}\!\cdot\!\sum_{k=1}^{n}\!\binom{n-1}{k-1}\frac{2^{k}}{k!}\cdot\!\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\cdot\frac{(2l)!\cdot S_{1}(k,2l+1)}{2^{2l+1}}\\[28.45274pt] \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x^{2n+1}\!\cdot\!\underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}\!\binom{2n}{k-1}\frac{2^{k}}{k!}\cdot\!\sum_{l=0}^{n}(-1)^{l}\cdot\frac{(2l)!\cdot S_{1}(k,2l+1)}{2^{2l+1}}}_{A_{n}}=\,x+\frac{1}{15}x^{5}+\frac{\,1}{45}x^{7}\\[28.45274pt] \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\phantom{mm}+\frac{\,64}{2835}x^{9}+\frac{\,71}{4725}x^{11}+\frac{\,5209}{405\,405}x^{13}+\frac{2\,203\,328}{212\,837\,625}x^{15}+\ldots\,,\quad\qquad|x|<1\,,\end{array}

where we used result (37), as well as the oddness of the expanded function.3030 30 Note that although the MacLaurin series for the arctangent is valid only in the unit circle, i.e. formally only for such xx that |arcthx|<1|\mathop{\rm arcth}\nolimits{x}|<1, the above expansion holds uniformly in the whole disk |x|<1|x|<1 (in virtue of the Cauchy’s theorem on the representation of analytic functions by power series, as well as of the principle of analytic continuation). Moreover, an advanced study of this series, analogous to that performed in the next section, shows that it also converges for x=1x=1. Inserting this expansion into (56) and performing the term–by–term integration, we obtain the following series for the difference of first two terms in curly brackets in (56)

ln⁡Γ⁡(1π)−lnΓ(12+1π)=12lnπ+1π∑n=0∞An2​n+1=12lnπ+1π{1+175+1315+6425 515+7151 975+52095 270 265+2 203 3283 192 564 375+132 313253 127 875+…}= 0.8988746544…\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\ln\Gamma\!\left(\!\dfrac{1}{\,\pi\,}\!\right)&\displaystyle-\ln\Gamma\!\left(\!\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{\,\pi\,}\!\right)=\frac{1}{2}\ln\pi+\frac{1}{\pi}\!\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{A_{n}}{2n+1}\,=\,\frac{1}{2}\ln\pi+\frac{1}{\pi}\left\{1+\frac{1}{75}+\frac{1}{315}+\frac{64}{25\,515}\right.\\[22.76219pt] &\displaystyle\!\!\!\!\!\!\left.+\,\frac{71}{51\,975}+\frac{5209}{5\,270\,265}+\frac{2\,203\,328}{3\,192\,564\,375}+\frac{132\,313}{253\,127\,875}+\ldots\right\}=\,0.8988746544\ldots\end{array} (57)

with AnA_{n} defined in the preceding equation. The derived series does not converge rapidly, see Fig. 1, but the most remarkable is that it contains rational coefficients only, which is quite unusual, especially for the arguments related to π−1\pi^{-1}.

This suggests that there might be some more general series similar in nature to (57), which allows to expand the logarithm of the Γ\Gamma–function at certain points related to π−1\pi^{-1} into the series with rational coefficients only. Such series expansions are the subject of our study in the next section.

III Series expansions for the logarithm of the Γ\Gamma–function and polygamma functions

III.1 First series expansion for the logarithm of the Γ\Gamma–function

III.1.1 Derivation of the series expansion

Consider the general form of the second Binet’s integral formula for the logarithm of the Γ\Gamma–function

∫0∞arc​tg⁡a​xeb​x−1​𝑑x=πb​ln⁡Γ⁡(b 2​π​a)+1 2​a​(1−ln⁡b2​π​a)+π 2​b​ln​b4​π2​a\int\limits_{0}^{\,\infty}\!\frac{\,\mathop{\mathrm{arc\,tg}}\nolimits{ax}\,}{e^{bx}-1}\,dx\,=\,\frac{\,\pi\,}{b}\ln\Gamma\!\left(\!\dfrac{b}{\,2\pi a\,}\!\right)+\frac{1}{\,2a\,}\!\left(1-\ln\frac{b}{2\pi a}\right)+\frac{\,\pi\,}{\,2b\,}\ln\frac{b}{4\pi^{2}a} (58)

a>0a>0\, and Reb>0\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits{b}>0\,, see e.g. [119, vol. I, no 2.7.5-6], [12, pp. 335–336], [160, pp. 250–251], [8, vol. I, p. 22, Eq. 1.9(9)] or [13, Sect. 4, exercise no 40]. The general idea of the method consists in finding such a change of variable that reduces the integrand in the left–hand side of (58) to a function (probably, a composite function) which may be “easily” expanded into the MacLaurin series. In our case, this change of variable may be easily found by requiring, for example, that

∫d​xeb​x−1=α​∫d​uu\int\!\frac{\,dx\,}{e^{bx}-1}\,=\,\alpha\!\int\!\frac{\,du\,}{u}

where uu is the new variable and α\alpha is some normalizing coefficient, which can be chosen later at our convenience. Other changes of variables, of course, are possible as well (see, e.g., numerous examples in exercises 39 & 45 [13, Sect. 4]), but this one is particularly successful, especially if we set α=1/b\alpha=1/b. Thus, putting x=−1b​ln⁡(1−u)\,x=-\frac{1}{b}\ln(1-u)\, and rewriting the result for z=b2​π​a\,z=\frac{b}{2\pi a}\,, Binet’s formula takes the form

−∫01arc​tg[1 2​π​zln(1−u)]d​uu=πlnΓ(z)+πz(1−lnz)+π 2lnz 2​π\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle-\!\int\limits_{0}^{1}\!\mathop{\mathrm{arc\,tg}}\nolimits{\!\Big[\frac{1}{\,2\pi z\,}\ln(1-u)\Big]}\frac{\,du\,}{u}\,=\,\pi\ln\Gamma(z)+\pi z(1-\ln z)+\frac{\,\pi\,}{\,2\,}\ln\frac{z}{\,2\pi\,}\end{array} (59)

where Rez>0\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits z>0. The integrand on the left may be expanded into the MacLaurin series in powers of uu accordingly to the method described in Section II. This yields

arc​tg⁡[1 2​π​z​ln⁡(1−u)]=∑l=0∞(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅[1 2​π​z​ln⁡(1−u)]2​l+1(2​l+1)!=−∑l=0∞(−1)l(2​l)!(2​π​z)2​l+1⋅∑n=2​l+1∞|S1​(n,2​l+1)|n!un=−∑n=1∞unn!⋅∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l(2​l)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(2​π​z)2​l+1\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\mathop{\mathrm{arc\,tg}}\nolimits{\!\Big[\frac{1}{\,2\pi z\,}\ln(1-u)\Big]}&\displaystyle\,=\,\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{l}(2l)!\cdot\frac{\left[\frac{1}{\,2\pi z\,}\ln(1-u)\right]^{2l+1}}{(2l+1)!}\\[14.22636pt] &\displaystyle=\,-\!\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{l}\frac{(2l)!}{\,(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}\,\cdot\!\!\!\!\sum_{n=2l+1}^{\infty}\!\!\!\!\frac{\,|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{\,n!\,}\,u^{n}\\[14.22636pt] &\displaystyle=\,-\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{u^{n}}{\,n!\,}\cdot\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{(2l)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|}{\,(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}\end{array} (60)

This expansion converges in the disk |u|<r|u|<r in which arc​tg⁡[1 2​π​z​ln⁡(1−u)]\,\mathop{\mathrm{arc\,tg}}\nolimits{\!\big[\frac{1}{\,2\pi z\,}\ln(1-u)\big]} is analytic. The radius of this disk rr depends on the parameter zz and is conditioned by the singularities of the arctangent, which occur at u=1−exp⁡(±2​π​i​z)u=1-\exp(\pm 2\pi iz) [branch points], and by that of the logarithm, which is located at u=1u=1 [branch point as well]. The latter restricts the value of rr to 1, and the unit radius of convergence corresponds to such zz that  2cos(2πRez)=exp(±2πImz)\,2\cos(2\pi\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits z\big)=\exp(\pm 2\pi\mathop{\rm Im}\nolimits z). The zone of convergence of series (60) for |u|<1|u|<1 consists, therefore, in the intersection of two zones, each of which lying to the right of curves

Imz=1 2​π⋅{+ln⁡2+ln⁡cos⁡(2​π​Rez)−ln⁡2−ln⁡cos⁡(2​π​Rez)\mathop{\rm Im}\nolimits{z}\,=\,\frac{1}{\,2\pi\,}\cdot\begin{cases}+\ln 2+\ln\cos\big(2\pi\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits z\big)\\[2.84526pt] -\ln 2-\ln\cos\big(2\pi\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits z\big)\\[2.84526pt] \end{cases} (61)

respectively, see Fig. 2.

Now, a close study of the general term of series (60) reveals that it also converges for u=1u=1. Indeed, from (74), it follows that one can always find such a constant C>1C>1 that for sufficiently large n0n_{0}, inequality

1n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(2​π​z)2​l+1⩽2​π​z​Cn​ln2​n,​n>n0,\frac{1}{\,n!\,}\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{(2l)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|}{\,(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}\,\leqslant\,\frac{2\pi z\,C}{\,n\ln^{2}\!n\,}\,,\qquad\quad\text{}n>n_{0}\,,

holds. Hence, since series ∑n−1​ln−α​n\,\sum n^{-1}\!\ln^{-\alpha}\!n converges for α>1\alpha>1, so does series (60) at u=1u=1. An interesting consequence of the latter statement is this curious identity

π2=∑n=1∞1n!⋅∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(2​π​z)2​l+1,\frac{\pi}{2}\,=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n!\,}\cdot\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{(2l)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|}{\,(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}\,, (62)

which holds in the region of convergence of zz. Thus, expansion (60) converges uniformly in each point of the disk |u|<1|u|<1 and can be integrated term--by--term.3131 31 Another way to show that (60) is uniformly convergent is to directly verify that ∫01[∑n=N∞unn!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(2​π​z)2​l+1]​𝑑u→ 0as ​N→∞\int\limits_{0}^{1}\!\left[\sum_{n=N}^{\infty}\!\frac{u^{n}}{\,n!\,}\!\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{(2l)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|}{\,(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}\right]du\,\to\,0\qquad\quad\text{as }\,N\to\infty see e.g. [149, pp. 161–162]. Substituting series (60) into (59) and performing the indicated term–by–term integration from u=0u=0\, to u=1\,u=1, we obtain the following series expansion for the logarithm of the Γ\Gamma–function

ln⁡Γ⁡(z)=(z−1 2)​ln⁡z−z+1 2​ln⁡2​π+1π​∑n=1∞1n⋅n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(2​π​z)2​l+1=(z−1 2)lnz−z+1 2ln2π+1π{12​π​z+18​π​z+118(1π​z−14​π3​z3)+396​(1π​z−12​π3​z3)+1600​(12π​z−354​π3​z3+34​π5​z5)+14320(60π​z−2254​π3​z3+454​π5​z5)+…}\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\ln\Gamma(z)&\displaystyle=\left(z-\frac{1}{\,2\,}\right)\!\ln z-z+\frac{1}{\,2\,}\ln 2\pi+\frac{1}{\,\pi\,}\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}\\[11.38109pt] &\displaystyle=\left(z-\frac{1}{\,2\,}\right)\!\ln z-z+\frac{1}{\,2\,}\ln 2\pi+\frac{1}{\,\pi\,}\left\{\frac{1}{2\pi z}+\frac{1}{8\pi z}+\frac{1}{18}\left(\frac{1}{\pi z}-\frac{1}{4\pi^{3}z^{3}}\right)\right.\\[11.38109pt] &\displaystyle\quad+\frac{3}{96}\left(\frac{1}{\pi z}-\frac{1}{2\pi^{3}z^{3}}\right)+\frac{1}{600}\left(\frac{12}{\pi z}-\frac{35}{4\pi^{3}z^{3}}+\frac{3}{4\pi^{5}z^{5}}\right)\\[11.38109pt] &\displaystyle\quad\left.+\frac{1}{4320}\left(\frac{60}{\pi z}-\frac{225}{4\pi^{3}z^{3}}+\frac{45}{4\pi^{5}z^{5}}\right)+\ldots\right\}\end{array} (63)

converging in the same region as series (60), see (61) and Fig. 2. In particular, if zz is real, it converges for z>16z>\frac{1}{6}; on the contrary, if zz is complex, then independently of its imaginary part, it converges everywhere in the right half–plane Rez⩾14\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits z\geqslant\frac{1}{4}. A quick analysis of the above series shows that for zz rational multiple of π−1\pi^{-1}, it contains rational coefficients only. Another important observation is that this series, unlike the classic Stirling series (I.1), cannot be explicitly written in powers of zz. To illustrate this point, we write down its first 2, 3 and 4 terms respectively:

∑n=1N1n⋅n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(2​π​z)2​l+1=={12​π​z+18​π​z=58​π​z,N=212​π​z+18​π​z+118(1π​z−14​π3​z3)=4972​π​z−172​π3​z3,N=312​π​z+18​π​z+118(1π​z−14​π3​z3)+396(1π​z−12​π3​z3)=205288​π​z−17576​π3​z3,N=4\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}=\\[17.07164pt] \displaystyle\qquad\,=\,\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{1}{2\pi z}+\frac{1}{8\pi z}\,=\,\frac{5}{8\pi z}\,,\qquad&N=2\\[11.38109pt] \displaystyle\frac{1}{2\pi z}+\frac{1}{8\pi z}+\frac{1}{18}\left(\frac{1}{\pi z}-\frac{1}{4\pi^{3}z^{3}}\right)\,=\,\frac{49}{72\pi z}-\frac{1}{72\pi^{3}z^{3}}\,,\qquad&N=3\\[11.38109pt] \displaystyle\frac{1}{2\pi z}+\frac{1}{8\pi z}+\frac{1}{18}\left(\frac{1}{\pi z}-\frac{1}{4\pi^{3}z^{3}}\right)+\frac{3}{96}\left(\frac{1}{\pi z}-\frac{1}{2\pi^{3}z^{3}}\right)\,=\,\frac{205}{288\pi z}-\frac{17}{576\pi^{3}z^{3}}\,,\qquad&N=4\end{cases}\end{array}

By the way, as concerns the divergent Stirling series (I.1), it can be readily derived from (63). By formally interchanging sum signs in (63), which is obviously not permitted because series are not absolutely convergent, we have

where we first used (42) for ζ⁡(2​l+2)\zeta(2l+2), and then, Euler’s formula

ζ(2l)=(−1)l+1(2​π)2​l⋅B2​l2⋅(2​l)!=(2​π)2​l⋅|B2​l|2⋅(2​l)!,l=1,2,3,…\zeta(2l)=(-1)^{l+1}\frac{\,(2\pi)^{2l}\cdot{B}_{2l}\,}{2\cdot(2l)!}\,=\,\frac{\,(2\pi)^{2l}\cdot|{B}_{2l}|\,}{2\cdot(2l)!}\,,\qquad\quad l=1,2,3,\ldots

Further observations concern the convergence of the derived series and are treated in details in the next section.

III.1.2 Convergence analysis of the derived series

The complete study of the convergence of (63) is quite long and complicated, that is why we split it in two stages. First, we obtain the upper bound for the general term of (63), and then, derive an accurate approximation for it when nn becomes sufficiently large. In what follows, we may suppose, without essential loss of generality, that zz is real and positive. The general term of series (63) is given by the finite sum over ll. This truncated sum has only odd terms, and hence, by elementary transformations, may be reduced to that containing both odd and even terms

∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(2​π​z)2​l+1=∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)12​(2​l+1)−12​(2​l+1)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(2​l+1)⋅(2​π​z)2​l+1=12​∑l=1n[1−(−1)l]⋅(−1)12​(l−1)⋅(l−1)!⋅|S1​(n,l)|(2​π​z)l=…\begin{array}[]{ll}&\displaystyle\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}=\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{\frac{1}{2}(2l+1)-\frac{1}{2}}\frac{\,(2l+1)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{(2l+1)\cdot(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}\\[14.22636pt] &\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad=\,\frac{1}{2}\!\sum_{l=1}^{n}\big[1-(-1)^{l}\big]\cdot(-1)^{\frac{1}{2}(l-1)}\cdot\frac{(l-1)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,l)|}{(2\pi z)^{l}}\,=\,\ldots\end{array} (64)

Now, from Legendre’s integral for the Euler Γ\Gamma--function,3232 32 Namely, (l+1)!=∫xl+1​e−x​𝑑x\,(l+1)!=\int\!x^{l+1}e^{-x}dx\, taken over x=[0,∞)x=[0,\infty). it follows that

{(−1)12​(l−1)⋅(l−1)!(2​π​z)l=−i∫0∞[i​x2​π​z]l⋅e−x​d​xx(−1)l⋅(−1)12​(l−1)⋅(l−1)!(2​π​z)l=−i∫0∞[−i​x2​π​z]l⋅e−x​d​xx\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle(-1)^{\frac{1}{2}(l-1)}\cdot\frac{\,(l-1)!\,}{(2\pi z)^{l}}\,=\,-i\!\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\!\left[\frac{i\,x}{2\pi z}\right]^{l}\!\cdot\frac{\,e^{-x}\,dx\,}{x}\\[17.07164pt] \displaystyle(-1)^{l}\cdot(-1)^{\frac{1}{2}(l-1)}\cdot\frac{\,(l-1)!\,}{(2\pi z)^{l}}\,=\,-i\!\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\!\left[-\frac{i\,x}{2\pi z}\right]^{l}\!\cdot\frac{\,e^{-x}\,dx\,}{x}\end{array}\right.

Hence, expression (64) may be continued as follows

…=i2​∫0∞∑l=1n{[−i​x2​π​z]l−[i​x2​π​z]l}​|S1​(n,l)|⋅e−x​d​xx=i2​∫0∞{(−i​x2​π​z)n−(i​x2​π​z)n}​e−x​d​xx=i 4​π2​z​∫0∞shx2​z​{Γ⁡(i​x2​π​z)​Γ​(n−i​x2​π​z)−Γ⁡(−i​x2​π​z)​Γ​(n+i​x2​π​z)}​e−x​𝑑x=−1 2​π2​z∫0∞shx2​z⋅e−x⋅Im[Γ(i​x2​π​z)Γ(n−i​x2​π​z)]dx\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\ldots&\displaystyle=\,\frac{i}{2}\!\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\!\sum_{l=1}^{n}\left\{\left[-\frac{i\,x}{2\pi z}\right]^{l}-\left[\frac{i\,x}{2\pi z}\right]^{l}\right\}|S_{1}(n,l)|\cdot\frac{\,e^{-x}\,dx\,}{x}\\[17.07164pt] &\displaystyle=\,\frac{i}{2}\!\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\!\left\{\!\left(-\frac{i\,x}{2\pi z}\right)_{\!n}-\left(\frac{i\,x}{2\pi z}\right)_{\!n}\!\right\}\frac{\,e^{-x}\,dx\,}{x}\\[14.22636pt] &\displaystyle=\,\frac{i}{\,4\pi^{2}z\,}\!\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\!\mathop{\rm sh}\nolimits\frac{x}{2z}\left\{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{i\,x}{2\pi z}\right)\Gamma\!\left(n-\frac{i\,x}{2\pi z}\right)-\Gamma\!\left(-\frac{i\,x}{2\pi z}\right)\Gamma\!\left(n+\frac{i\,x}{2\pi z}\right)\!\right\}e^{-x}\,dx\\[17.07164pt] &\displaystyle=\,-\frac{1}{\,2\pi^{2}z\,}\!\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\!\mathop{\rm sh}\nolimits\frac{x}{2z}\cdot e^{-x}\cdot\mathop{\rm Im}\nolimits\left[\Gamma\!\left(\frac{i\,x}{2\pi z}\right)\Gamma\!\left(n-\frac{i\,x}{2\pi z}\right)\!\right]dx\end{array} (65)

1n⋅n!|∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l(2​l)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(2​π​z)2​l+1|⩽1n2⋅ 1π∫0∞shtt⋅e−2​z​tdt\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\left|\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}\right|\leqslant\,\frac{1}{\,n^{2}\,}\cdot\frac{\,1\,}{\,\pi\,}\!\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\!\sqrt{\frac{\mathop{\rm sh}\nolimits t\,}{\,t\,}}\cdot e^{-2zt}\,dt (67)

where the latter integral converges uniformly in the half–plane zz which lies to the right of the line Rez=14\,\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits z=\frac{1}{4} (imaginary part of zz contributes only to the bounded oscillations of the integrand). Consequently, series (63) converges at least in Rez>14\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits z>\frac{1}{4}, and this at the same rate or better than Euler’s series ∑n−2\,\sum n^{-2}.

Numerical simulations show, however, that the greater nn, the greater the relative difference between the upper bound and the left–hand side in (67), see Fig. 3,

and thus, this upper bound is relatively rough.3333 33 The error is mainly due to the use of inequality |ImΓ⁡(v)|⩽|Γ⁡(v)|\,|\mathop{\rm Im}\nolimits\Gamma(v)|\leqslant|\Gamma(v)|\,. A more accurate description of the behavior of sum (64) at large nn may be obtained by seeking its asymptotics. In order to find it, we proceed as follows. ∫0∞Im[(i​x2​π​z)n]​e−x​d​xx∼(n−1)!​∑k=0∞(−1)k​a2​k+1​(2​k)!(2​π​z)2​k+1⋅cos⁡[(2​k+1)​arc​tg⁡ln⁡n2​π​z][1+ln2⁡n4​π2​z2]k+12+(n−1)!∑k=1∞(−1)ka2​k(2​k−1)!(2​π​z)2​k⋅sin⁡[2​k​arc​tg⁡ln⁡n2​π​z][1+ln2⁡n4​π2​z2]k\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\!\mathop{\rm Im}\nolimits\left[\!\left(\frac{i\,x}{2\pi z}\right)_{\!n}\right]\frac{\,e^{-x}\,dx\,}{x}\,\sim\,(n-1)!\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{k}a_{2k+1}\frac{(2k)!}{(2\pi z)^{2k+1}}\cdot\frac{\cos\left[(2k+1)\mathop{\mathrm{arc\,tg}}\nolimits\dfrac{\ln n}{2\pi z}\right]}{\left[1+\dfrac{\ln^{2}\!n}{4\pi^{2}z^{2}}\right]^{k+\frac{1}{2}}}\\[34.1433pt] \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+(n-1)!\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{k}a_{2k}\frac{(2k-1)!}{(2\pi z)^{2k}}\cdot\frac{\sin\left[2k\mathop{\mathrm{arc\,tg}}\nolimits\dfrac{\ln n}{2\pi z}\right]}{\left[1+\dfrac{\ln^{2}\!n}{4\pi^{2}z^{2}}\right]^{k}}\end{array}

Whence, the required asymptotics is

1n⋅n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(2​π​z)2​l+1==1n2​∑k=0∞(−1)k(2​k+1)​(4​π2​z2+ln2⁡n)k+12⋅cos⁡[(2​k+1)​arc​tg⁡ln⁡n2​π​z]⋅[1Γ⁡(x)]x=0(2​k+1)+1n2∑k=1∞(−1)k 2​k​(4​π2​z2+ln2⁡n)k⋅sin[2karc​tgln⁡n2​π​z]⋅[1Γ⁡(x)](2​k)x=0+O(1n3)\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}\,=\\[17.07164pt] \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\quad=\frac{1}{\,n^{2}\,}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{\,(2k+1)\big(4\pi^{2}z^{2}+\ln^{2}\!n\big)^{k+\frac{1}{2}}\,}\cdot\cos\left[(2k+1)\mathop{\mathrm{arc\,tg}}\nolimits\dfrac{\ln n}{2\pi z}\right]\cdot\left[\frac{1}{\Gamma(x)}\right]^{(2k+1)}_{x=0}\\[28.45274pt] \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad+\frac{1}{\,n^{2}\,}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{\,2k\big(4\pi^{2}z^{2}+\ln^{2}\!n\big)^{k}\,}\cdot\sin\left[2k\mathop{\mathrm{arc\,tg}}\nolimits\dfrac{\ln n}{2\pi z}\right]\cdot\left[\frac{1}{\Gamma(x)}\right]^{(2k)}_{x=0}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{n^{3}}\right)\end{array} (73)

for sufficiently large nn. Retaining first few terms, we have

1n⋅n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(2​π​z)2​l+1= 2​π​zn2​{1 4​π2​z2+ln2⁡n−2​γ​ln⁡n(4​π2​z2+ln2⁡n)2}+O⁡(1n2​ln4​n),n→∞\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}\,=\,\frac{\,2\pi z\,}{n^{2}}\left\{\frac{1}{\,4\pi^{2}z^{2}+\ln^{2}\!n\,}-\frac{2\gamma\ln n}{\,\big(4\pi^{2}z^{2}+\ln^{2}\!n\big)^{2}\,}\right\}\\[17.07164pt] \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+\,O\!\left(\frac{1}{n^{2}\ln^{4}\!n}\right)\,,\qquad n\to\infty\end{array} (74)

Thus, for moderate values of zz, series (63) converges approximately at the same rate as ∑(n​ln⁡n)−2\,\sum(n\ln n)^{-2}, i.e. at the same rate as, for example, Fontana–Mascheroni’s series (12), (47), see asymptotics (21).

III.1.3 Some important particular cases of the derived series

Let now consider some applications of the formula (63). In the first instance, it is natural to obtain a series expansion for

ln⁡Γ⁡(1π)=(1−1π)⋅ln⁡π−1π+12​ln⁡2+12​π​∑n=1∞1n⋅n!⋅{∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|22​l}=(1−1π)⋅ln⁡π−1π+12​ln⁡2+12​π​{1+14+112+132+175+1144+132880+15746 080+…}\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\ln\Gamma\!\left(\!\dfrac{1}{\,\pi\,}\!\right)&\displaystyle=\left(\!1-\frac{1}{\pi}\!\right)\!\cdot\ln\pi-\frac{1}{\pi}+\frac{1}{2}\ln 2+\frac{1}{2\pi}\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\cdot\Biggl\{\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{(2l)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|}{2^{2l}}\Biggr\}\\[17.07164pt] &\displaystyle\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!=\left(\!1-\frac{1}{\pi}\!\right)\!\cdot\ln\pi-\frac{1}{\pi}+\frac{1}{2}\ln 2+\frac{1}{2\pi}\left\{1+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{32}+\frac{1}{75}+\frac{1}{144}+\frac{13}{2880}+\frac{157}{46\,080}+\ldots\right\}\end{array} (75)

The graphical illustration of the convergence of this series is given in Fig. 4. With equal ease, we derive

ln⁡Γ⁡(2π)=(1−2π)⋅ln⁡π−2π+2π​ln⁡2+14​π​∑n=1∞1n⋅n!⋅{∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|24​l}=(1−2π)⋅ln⁡π−2π+2π​ln⁡2+14​π​{1+14+548+7128+63119 200+1999216+19 5011 290 240+32 7072 949 120+…}\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\ln\Gamma\!\left(\!\dfrac{2}{\,\pi\,}\!\right)&\displaystyle=\left(\!1-\frac{2}{\pi}\!\right)\!\cdot\ln\pi-\frac{2}{\pi}+\frac{2}{\pi}\ln 2+\frac{1}{4\pi}\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\cdot\Biggl\{\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{(2l)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|}{2^{4l}}\Biggr\}\\[17.07164pt] &\displaystyle\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!=\left(\!1-\frac{2}{\pi}\!\right)\!\cdot\ln\pi-\frac{2}{\pi}+\frac{2}{\pi}\ln 2+\frac{1}{4\pi}\left\{1+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{5}{48}+\frac{7}{128}+\frac{631}{19\,200}+\frac{199}{9216}+\frac{19\,501}{1\,290\,240}+\frac{32\,707}{2\,949\,120}+\ldots\right\}\end{array} (76)

Many other similar expansions may be derived analogously. Let now see how the series behaves outside the region of convergence. For this aim, we take z=12​π−1z=\frac{1}{2}\pi^{-1}. Formula (63) yields

ln⁡Γ⁡(1 2​π)=?(1−12​π)⋅ln⁡2​π−12​π+1π​∑n=1∞1n⋅n!⋅{∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|}=(1−12​π)⋅ln⁡2​π−12​π+1π​{1+14−116−11300+1144+17630+1015760−311102 060−…}\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\ln\Gamma\!\left(\!\dfrac{1}{\,2\pi\,}\!\right)&\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}\left(\!1-\frac{1}{2\pi}\!\right)\!\cdot\ln 2\pi-\frac{1}{2\pi}+\frac{1}{\pi}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\cdot\Biggl\{\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}(2l)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\Biggr\}\\[17.07164pt] &\displaystyle=\left(\!1-\frac{1}{2\pi}\!\right)\!\cdot\ln 2\pi-\frac{1}{2\pi}+\frac{1}{\pi}\left\{1+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16}-\frac{11}{300}+\frac{1}{144}+\frac{17}{630}+\frac{101}{5760}-\frac{311}{102\,060}-\ldots\right\}\end{array} (77)

At first sight, it might seem that this alternating series slowly converges to ln⁡Γ⁡(12​π−1)≈1.765383194\ln\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}\pi^{-1})\approx 1.765383194: the summation of its first 3 terms gives the value 1.764207893​…1.764207893\ldots which corresponds to the relative accuracy ×10−46.6\!\times\!10^{-4}, that of 18 terms gives 1.765525087​…1.765525087\ldots, i.e. the relative accuracy ×10−58.0\!\times\!10^{-5}, the summation of first 32 terms yields 1.765392783​…1.765392783\ldots which corresponds to the relative error ×10−65.4\!\times\!10^{-6}.3636 36 We do not count the third term which is zero. Notwithstanding, further numerical simulations, see Fig. 5, leave no doubts: this series is divergent.

III.2 Second series expansion for the logarithm of the Γ\Gamma–function

Rewrite formula (63) for 2​z2z instead of zz, and subtract the result from (63). In virtue of Legendre’s duplication formula for the Γ\Gamma–function ln⁡Γ⁡(2​z)=(2​z−1)​ln⁡2−12​ln⁡π+ln⁡Γ⁡(z)+ln⁡Γ⁡(z+12)\ln\Gamma(2z)=(2z-1)\ln 2-\frac{1}{2}\ln\pi+\ln\Gamma(z)+\ln\Gamma(z+\frac{1}{2}), we have

ln⁡Γ⁡(12+z)=z​ln⁡z−z+1 2​ln⁡2​π−1π​∑n=1∞1n⋅n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅(22​l+1−1)⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(4​π​z)2​l+1=zlnz−z+1 2ln2π−1π{14​π​z+116​π​z+118(12​π​z−732​π3​z3)+396(12​π​z−716​π3​z3)+1600(6π​z−24532​π3​z3+93128​π5​z5)+14320(30π​z−157532​π3​z3+1395128​π5​z5)+…}\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\ln\Gamma\!\left(\frac{1}{2}+z\right)&\displaystyle=\,z\ln{z}-z+\frac{1}{\,2\,}\ln 2\pi-\frac{1}{\,\pi\,}\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l)!\cdot(2^{2l+1}-1)\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{(4\pi z)^{2l+1}}\\[14.22636pt] &\displaystyle\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!=\,z\ln{z}-z+\frac{1}{\,2\,}\ln 2\pi-\frac{1}{\,\pi\,}\left\{\frac{1}{4\pi z}+\frac{1}{16\pi z}+\frac{1}{18}\left(\frac{1}{2\pi z}-\frac{7}{32\pi^{3}z^{3}}\right)+\frac{3}{96}\left(\frac{1}{2\pi z}-\frac{7}{16\pi^{3}z^{3}}\right)\right.\\[14.22636pt] &\displaystyle\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\quad\left.+\frac{1}{600}\left(\frac{6}{\pi z}-\frac{245}{32\pi^{3}z^{3}}+\frac{93}{128\pi^{5}z^{5}}\right)+\frac{1}{4320}\left(\frac{30}{\pi z}-\frac{1575}{32\pi^{3}z^{3}}+\frac{1395}{128\pi^{5}z^{5}}\right)+\ldots\right\}\end{array} (78)

which holds in the green zone shown in Fig. 2. This expression allows to expand any value of the form ln⁡Γ⁡(12+α​π−1)\ln\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}+\alpha\pi^{-1}) into the series with rational coefficients if α\alpha is rational greater than 16​π\frac{1}{6}\pi. For example, putting z=π−1z=\pi^{-1}, we have

ln⁡Γ⁡(12+1π)\displaystyle\displaystyle\ln\Gamma\!\left(\!\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{\,\pi\,}\!\right)\; =−1+ln⁡ππ+1 2​ln⁡2​π−1 4​π​∑n=1∞1n⋅n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅(22​l+1−1)⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|24​l\displaystyle\displaystyle=\,-\frac{1+\ln\pi}{\pi}+\frac{1}{\,2\,}\ln 2\pi-\frac{1}{\,4\pi\,}\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l)!\cdot(2^{2l+1}-1)\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{2^{4l}}
=−1+ln⁡ππ+1 2​ln⁡2​π−1 4​π​{1+14+116+1128−11919 200−719216−78531 290 240−12 6112 949 120−…}\displaystyle\displaystyle\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!=\,-\frac{1+\ln\pi}{\pi}+\frac{1}{\,2\,}\ln 2\pi-\frac{1}{\,4\pi\,}\!\left\{1+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{128}-\frac{119}{19\,200}-\frac{71}{9216}-\frac{7853}{1\,290\,240}-\frac{12\,611}{2\,949\,120}-\ldots\right\}

Furthermore, both series expansions (63) and (78), used together with the reflection formula and the recurrence relationship for the Γ\Gamma–function, yield series with rational coefficients for any values of the form ln⁡Γ⁡(12​n±α​π−1)\ln\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}n\pm\alpha\pi^{-1}), where nn is integer.

As a final remark, we note that expression (78), written for zz instead of 12+z\frac{1}{2}+z, straightforwardly produces another series expansion for the logarithm of the Γ\Gamma–function

ln⁡Γ⁡(z)=\displaystyle\displaystyle\ln\Gamma(z)= (z−1 2)​ln⁡(z−1 2)−z+1 2+1 2​ln⁡2​π\displaystyle\displaystyle\left(z-\frac{1}{\,2\,}\right)\!\ln\!{\left(z-\frac{1}{\,2\,}\right)}-z+\frac{1}{\,2\,}+\frac{1}{\,2\,}\ln 2\pi (79)
−1π∑n=1∞1n⋅n!∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l(2​l)!⋅(22​l+1−1)⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(4​π)2​l+1⋅(z−12)2​l+1\displaystyle\displaystyle-\frac{1}{\,\pi\,}\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l)!\cdot(2^{2l+1}-1)\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{(4\pi)^{2l+1}\cdot\big(z-\frac{1}{2}\big)^{2l+1}}

which converges in the green zone given in Fig. 2 shifted by 12\frac{1}{2} to the right. In particular, if zz is real, it converges for any z>23z>\frac{2}{3}.

Remark Expansion (78) may be also derived if we replace in (58) Binet’s formula by its analog with “conjugated” denominator

∫0∞arc​tg⁡a​xeb​x+1​𝑑x=−πb​ln⁡Γ⁡(12+b 2​π​a)−1 2​a​(1+ln⁡2​π​ab)+π 2​b​ln​2​π.\int\limits_{0}^{\,\infty}\!\frac{\,\mathop{\mathrm{arc\,tg}}\nolimits{ax}\,}{e^{bx}+1}\,dx\,=\,-\frac{\,\pi\,}{b}\ln\Gamma\!\left(\!\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{b}{\,2\pi a\,}\!\right)-\frac{1}{\,2a\,}\!\left(1+\ln\frac{2\pi a}{b}\right)+\frac{\,\pi\,}{\,2b\,}\ln 2\pi.

where a>0a>0 and Reb>0\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits{b}>0, see [13, Sect. 4, exercise no 40-a], or if we replace it by the following formula

∫0∞arc​tg⁡a​xshb​x​𝑑x=πb​{ln⁡Γ⁡(b 2​π​a)−ln⁡Γ⁡(12+b 2​π​a)−12​ln​2​π​ab}\int\limits_{0}^{\,\infty}\!\frac{\,\mathop{\mathrm{arc\,tg}}\nolimits{ax}\,}{\mathop{\rm sh}\nolimits{bx}}\,dx\,=\,\frac{\,\pi\,}{b}\left\{\ln\Gamma\!\left(\!\dfrac{b}{\,2\pi a\,}\!\right)-\ln\Gamma\!\left(\!\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{b}{\,2\pi a\,}\!\right)-\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{2\pi a}{b}\right\}

derived in [13, Sect. 4, exercise no 39-e]. Making a change of variable x=−2barcthu\,x=-\frac{2}{b}\mathop{\rm arcth}\nolimits u\,, and then, proceeding analogously to (59)–(63), yields

ln⁡Γ⁡(z)−ln⁡Γ⁡(12+z)=−12​ln​z+1π​∑n=0∞1 2​n+1​∑k=12​n+12kk!​(2​nk−1)​∑l=0n(−1)l​(2​l)!⋅S1​(k,2​l+1)(2​π​z)2​l+1\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle\ln\Gamma(z)-\ln\Gamma\!\left(\frac{1}{2}+z\right)=\,-\frac{1}{2}\ln{z}+\frac{1}{\pi}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\,2n+1\,}\!\sum_{k=1}^{2n+1}\frac{2^{k}}{k!}\binom{2n}{k-1}\sum_{l=0}^{n}(-1)^{l}\frac{(2l)!\cdot S_{1}(k,2l+1)}{(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}\end{array} (80)

which, being combined with (78), leads to a rearranged version of (63).

III.3 Series expansion for the polygamma functions

By differentiating expressions (63) and (79), one may easily deduce similar series expansions for the polygamma functions. Differentiating the former expansion yields the following series representations for the digamma and trigamma functions

Ψ⁡(z)=ln⁡z−1 2​z−1π​z​∑n=1∞1n⋅n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l+1)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(2​π​z)2​l+1=lnz−1 2​z−1π​z{12​π​z+18​π​z+118(1π​z−34​π3​z3)+396(1π​z−32​π3​z3)+1600(12π​z−1054​π3​z3+154​π5​z5)+14320(60π​z−6754​π3​z3+2254​π5​z5)+…}\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\Psi(z)&\displaystyle=\,\ln z-\frac{1}{\,2z\,}-\frac{1}{\,\pi z\,}\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l+1)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}\\[14.22636pt] &\displaystyle=\,\ln z-\frac{1}{\,2z\,}-\frac{1}{\,\pi z\,}\left\{\frac{1}{2\pi z}+\frac{1}{8\pi z}+\frac{1}{18}\left(\frac{1}{\pi z}-\frac{3}{4\pi^{3}z^{3}}\right)+\frac{3}{96}\left(\frac{1}{\pi z}-\frac{3}{2\pi^{3}z^{3}}\right)\right.\\[14.22636pt] &\displaystyle\quad\left.+\frac{1}{600}\left(\frac{12}{\pi z}-\frac{105}{4\pi^{3}z^{3}}+\frac{15}{4\pi^{5}z^{5}}\right)+\frac{1}{4320}\left(\frac{60}{\pi z}-\frac{675}{4\pi^{3}z^{3}}+\frac{225}{4\pi^{5}z^{5}}\right)+\ldots\right\}\end{array} (81)

and

Ψ1​(z)=1 2​z2+1z+1π​z2​∑n=1∞1n⋅n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l+2)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(2​π​z)2​l+1=1 2​z2+1z+1π​z2{1π​z+14​π​z+118(2π​z−3π3​z3)+396(2π​z−6π3​z3)+1600(24π​z−105π3​z3+452​π5​z5)+14320(120π​z−675π3​z3+6752​π5​z5)+…}\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\Psi_{1}(z)&\displaystyle=\,\frac{1}{\,2z^{2}\,}+\frac{1}{\,z\,}+\frac{1}{\,\pi z^{2}\,}\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l+2)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}\\[14.22636pt] &\displaystyle=\,\frac{1}{\,2z^{2}\,}+\frac{1}{\,z\,}+\frac{1}{\,\pi z^{2}\,}\left\{\frac{1}{\pi z}+\frac{1}{4\pi z}+\frac{1}{18}\left(\frac{2}{\pi z}-\frac{3}{\pi^{3}z^{3}}\right)+\frac{3}{96}\left(\frac{2}{\pi z}-\frac{6}{\pi^{3}z^{3}}\right)\right.\\[14.22636pt] &\displaystyle\quad\left.+\frac{1}{600}\left(\frac{24}{\pi z}-\frac{105}{\pi^{3}z^{3}}+\frac{45}{2\pi^{5}z^{5}}\right)+\frac{1}{4320}\left(\frac{120}{\pi z}-\frac{675}{\pi^{3}z^{3}}+\frac{675}{2\pi^{5}z^{5}}\right)+\ldots\right\}\end{array} (82)

respectively. More generally, by differentiating kk times with respect to zz the above series for Ψ⁡(z)\Psi(z), we obtain a series expansion for the kkth polygamma function

Ψk​(z)=(−1)k+1​k! 2​zk+1+(−1)k+1​(k−1)!zk+(−1)k+1π​zk+1​∑n=1∞1n⋅n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l+k+1)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(2​π​z)2​l+1=(−1)k+1k! 2​zk+1+(−1)k+1(k−1)!zk+(−1)k+1π​zk+1{(k+1)!2​π​z+(k+1)!8​π​z+118[(k+1)!π​z−(k+3)!8​π3​z3]+396[(k+1)!π​z−(k+3)!4​π3​z3]+1600[12​(k+1)!π​z−35​(k+3)!8​π3​z3+(k+5)!32​π5​z5]+…}\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\Psi_{k}(z)&\displaystyle=\,(-1)^{k+1}\frac{k!}{\,2z^{k+1}\,}+(-1)^{k+1}\frac{(k-1)!}{\,z^{k}\,}+\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{\,\pi z^{k+1}\,}\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l+k+1)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{(2\pi z)^{2l+1}}\\[14.22636pt] &\displaystyle=\,(-1)^{k+1}\frac{k!}{\,2z^{k+1}\,}+(-1)^{k+1}\frac{(k-1)!}{\,z^{k}\,}+\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{\,\pi z^{k+1}\,}\!\left\{\frac{(k+1)!}{2\pi z}+\frac{(k+1)!}{8\pi z}+\frac{1}{18}\left[\frac{(k+1)!}{\pi z}-\frac{(k+3)!}{8\pi^{3}z^{3}}\right]\right.\\[14.22636pt] &\displaystyle\quad\left.+\frac{3}{96}\left[\frac{(k+1)!}{\pi z}-\frac{(k+3)!}{4\pi^{3}z^{3}}\right]+\frac{1}{600}\left[\frac{12\,(k+1)!}{\pi z}-\frac{35\,(k+3)!}{8\pi^{3}z^{3}}+\frac{(k+5)!}{32\pi^{5}z^{5}}\right]+\ldots\right\}\end{array} (83)

where k=1,2,3,…k=1,2,3,\ldots Convergence analysis of these series is analogous to that performed in Section III.1.2, and we omit the details because the calculations are a little bit long. This analysis reveals that the general term of these series may be always bounded by αk​(z)​n−2\alpha_{k}(z)n^{-2}, where αk​(z)\alpha_{k}(z) depends solely on zz and on the order of the polygamma function kk. At large nn, the general term of these series is of the same order as (n​lnm​n)−2\big(n\ln^{m}\!n\big)^{-2}, where m=1m=1 for Ψ⁡(z)\Psi(z), m=2m=2 for Ψ1​(z)\Psi_{1}(z) and Ψ2​(z)\Psi_{2}(z), m=3m=3 for Ψ3​(z)\Psi_{3}(z) and Ψ4​(z)\Psi_{4}(z), and so on.

We now give several particular cases of the above expansions. From (81)–(83), it follows that at π−1\pi^{-1}, the polygamma functions have the following series representations

Ψ⁡(1π)=−ln⁡π−π 2−∑n=1∞1n⋅n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l+1)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|22​l+1=−ln⁡π−π 2−12−18−172+164+7400+7576+64394 080+10330 720+…\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\Psi\!\left(\!\dfrac{1}{\,\pi\,}\!\right)&\displaystyle=\,-\ln\pi-\frac{\pi}{\,2\,}-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l+1)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{2^{2l+1}}\\[17.07164pt] &\displaystyle=-\ln\pi-\frac{\pi}{\,2\,}-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{8}-\frac{1}{72}+\frac{1}{64}+\frac{7}{400}+\frac{7}{576}+\frac{643}{94\,080}+\frac{103}{30\,720}+\ldots\end{array} (84)
Ψ1​(1π)=π2 2+π+π​∑n=1∞1n⋅n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l+2)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|22​l+1=π2 2+π+π⁡{1+14−118−18−39400−29576−35323 520+113840+…}\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\Psi_{1}\!\left(\!\dfrac{1}{\,\pi\,}\!\right)&\displaystyle=\,\frac{\pi^{2}}{\,2\,}+\pi+\pi\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l+2)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{2^{2l+1}}\\[17.07164pt] &\displaystyle=\,\frac{\pi^{2}}{\,2\,}+\pi+\pi\left\{1+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{18}-\frac{1}{8}-\frac{39}{400}-\frac{29}{576}-\frac{353}{23\,520}+\frac{11}{3840}+\ldots\right\}\end{array} (85)

and, more generally, for k=1,2,3,…k=1,2,3,\ldots\,

Ψk​(1π)=(−1)k+1​πk⋅{π​k! 2+(k−1)!+∑n=1∞1n⋅n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l+k+1)!⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|22​l+1}=(−1)k+1πk⋅{π​k! 2+(k−1)!+(1+k)!2+(1+k)!8+118[(k+1)!−(k+3)!8]+396[(k+1)!−(k+3)!4]+1600[12(k+1)!−35​(k+3)!8+(k+5)!32]+…}\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\Psi_{k}\!\left(\!\dfrac{1}{\,\pi\,}\!\right)&\displaystyle=\,(-1)^{k+1}\pi^{k}\cdot\left\{\frac{\pi\,k!}{\,2\,}+(k-1)!+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l+k+1)!\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{2^{2l+1}}\right\}\\[17.07164pt] &\displaystyle=\,(-1)^{k+1}\pi^{k}\cdot\left\{\frac{\pi\,k!}{\,2\,}+(k-1)!+\frac{(1+k)!}{2}+\frac{(1+k)!}{8}+\frac{1}{18}\left[(k+1)!-\frac{(k+3)!}{8}\right]\right.\\[17.07164pt] &\displaystyle\quad\left.+\frac{3}{96}\left[(k+1)!-\frac{(k+3)!}{4}\right]+\frac{1}{600}\left[12\,(k+1)!-\frac{35\,(k+3)!}{8}+\frac{(k+5)!}{32}\right]+\ldots\right\}\end{array} (86)

Figure 6 shows the rate of convergence of first two series.

Second variant of the series expansions for the polygamma functions follows from (79). Differentiating the latter with respect to zz yields

Ψ⁡(z)=ln⁡(z−1 2)+1π​∑n=1∞1n⋅n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l+1)!⋅(22​l+1−1)⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(4​π)2​l+1⋅(z−12)2​l+2\Psi(z)\,=\,\ln\!{\left(z-\frac{1}{\,2\,}\right)}+\frac{1}{\,\pi\,}\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l+1)!\cdot(2^{2l+1}-1)\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{(4\pi)^{2l+1}\cdot\big(z-\frac{1}{2}\big)^{2l+2}}\vskip-4.2679pt (87)

and

Ψk​(z)=(−1)k+1​(k−1)!(z−12)k+(−1)kπ​∑n=1∞1n⋅n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l+k+1)!⋅(22​l+1−1)⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|(4​π)2​l+1⋅(z−12)2​l+k+2\Psi_{k}(z)\,=\,\frac{\,(-1)^{k+1}(k-1)!\,}{\big(z-\frac{1}{2}\big)^{k}}+\frac{(-1)^{k}}{\,\pi\,}\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l+k+1)!\cdot(2^{2l+1}-1)\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{(4\pi)^{2l+1}\cdot\big(z-\frac{1}{2}\big)^{2l+k+2}} (88)

In particular,

Ψ⁡(1 2+1π)=−ln⁡π+∑n=1∞1n⋅n!​∑l=0⌊12​n⌋(−1)l​(2​l+1)!⋅(22​l+1−1)⋅|S1​(n,2​l+1)|24​l+2=−ln⁡π+14+116−5576−13512−56925 600−53936 864−98 67112 042 240−…\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle\Psi\!\left(\!\dfrac{1}{\,2\,}+\dfrac{1}{\,\pi\,}\!\right)&\displaystyle=\,-\ln\pi+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1}{\,n\cdot n!\,}\!\sum_{l=0}^{\lfloor\frac{1}{2}n\rfloor}\!(-1)^{l}\frac{\,(2l+1)!\cdot(2^{2l+1}-1)\cdot|S_{1}(n,2l+1)|\,}{2^{4l+2}}\\[17.07164pt] &\displaystyle=-\ln\pi+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{16}-\frac{5}{576}-\frac{13}{512}-\frac{569}{25\,600}-\frac{539}{36\,864}-\frac{98\,671}{12\,042\,240}-\ldots\end{array} (89)

Similarly to expansions for ln⁡Γ⁡(z)\ln\Gamma(z), expansions (83) and (88), combined with the reflection formula and the recurrence relationship for polygamma functions, give series with rational coefficients for any polygamma function of the argument 12​n±α​π−1\,\frac{1}{2}n\pm\alpha\pi^{-1}\,, where α\alpha is rational greater than 16​π\frac{1}{6}\pi and nn is integer.

Final remark Series which we discovered in the present work are very interesting especially because of the implication of combinatorial numbers S1​(n,l)S_{1}(n,l). In this context, it seems appropriate to note that series of a similar nature for ln⁡Γ⁡(z)\ln\Gamma(z) and Ψk​(z)\Psi_{k}(z) were already obtained, but remain little–known and practically not mentioned in modern literature. For instance, in 1839, Jacques Binet [12, pp. 231–236, 257, 237, 235, 335–339, Eqs. (63), (81)] obtained several, rapidly convergent for large |z||z|, expansions

ln⁡Γ⁡(z)=(z−1 2)​ln⁡z−z+1 2​ln⁡2​π+12​∑n=1∞I⁡(n)n⋅1(z+1)nln⁡Γ⁡(z)=(z−1 2)​ln⁡z−z+1 2​ln⁡2​π−12​∑n=1∞I′​(n)n⋅1(z)nΨ⁡(z)=ln⁡z−12​z−12​∑n=2∞K⁡(n)n⋅1(z+1)nΨ⁡(z)=ln⁡z−12​z−12​∑n=2∞K⁡(n)−n​K​(n−1)n⋅1(z)n\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle\ln\Gamma(z)\,=\,\left(z-\frac{1}{\,2\,}\right)\!\ln z-z+\frac{1}{\,2\,}\ln 2\pi+\frac{1}{2}\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{I(n)}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{(z+1)_{n}}\\[14.22636pt] \displaystyle\ln\Gamma(z)\,=\,\left(z-\frac{1}{\,2\,}\right)\!\ln z-z+\frac{1}{\,2\,}\ln 2\pi-\frac{1}{2}\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{I^{\prime}(n)}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{(z)_{n}}\\[14.22636pt] \displaystyle\Psi(z)\,=\,\ln z-\frac{1}{2z}-\frac{1}{2}\!\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\!\frac{K(n)}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{(z+1)_{n}}\\[14.22636pt] \displaystyle\Psi(z)\,=\,\ln z-\frac{1}{2z}-\frac{1}{2}\!\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\!\frac{K(n)-nK(n-1)}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{(z)_{n}}\end{array} (90)

where numbers I⁡(n)I(n), I′​(n)I^{\prime}(n) and K⁡(n)K(n) are rational and may be given in terms of the Stirling numbers of the first kind. Binet recognized these numbers, denoted them by a capital HH, referenced Stirling’s treatise [146] and even corrected Striling’s error: in the table on p. 11 [146] he noticed that the value of |S1​(9,3)|=118 124|S_{1}(9,3)|=118\,124 and not 105 056105\,056. In our notations, Binet’s formulæ for I⁡(n)I(n), I′​(n)I^{\prime}(n) and K⁡(n)K(n) read

I⁡(n)=∫01(2​x−1)​(x)n​𝑑x=∑l=1nl⋅|S1​(n,l)|(l+1)​(l+2)=∑l=1n|S1​(n,l)|l+2−C2,nI′​(n)=∫01(2​x−1)​(1−x)​(x)n−1​𝑑x=∑l=1n−2l⋅|S1​(n−1,l+1)|(l+2)​(l+3)​(l+4)K⁡(n)=n!−∫01(x)n​𝑑x=n!−∑l=1n|S1​(n,l)|l+1=n!−2​C2,n\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle I(n)\,=\int\limits_{0}^{1}\!(2x-1)(x)_{n}\,dx=\sum_{l=1}^{n}\frac{l\cdot\big|S_{1}(n,l)\big|}{(l+1)(l+2)}\,=\,2\!\sum_{l=1}^{n}\frac{\big|S_{1}(n,l)\big|}{\,l+2\,}\,-\ \,C_{2,n}\\[14.22636pt] \displaystyle I^{\prime}(n)\,=\int\limits_{0}^{1}\!(2x-1)(1-x)(x)_{n-1}\,dx=\sum_{l=1}^{n-2}\frac{l\cdot\big|S_{1}(n-1,l+1)\big|}{(l+2)(l+3)(l+4)}\\[14.22636pt] \displaystyle K(n)\,=\,n!-2\!\int\limits_{0}^{1}\!(x)_{n}\,dx=\,n!-2\!\sum_{l=1}^{n}\frac{\big|S_{1}(n,l)\big|}{\,l+1\,}\,=\,n!-2C_{2,n}\end{array} (91)

In particular, the first few coefficients are I⁡(1)=16I(1)=\frac{1}{6}, I⁡(2)=13I(2)=\frac{1}{3}, I⁡(3)=5960I(3)=\frac{59}{60}, I⁡(4)=5815I(4)=\frac{58}{15}, I⁡(5)=53328I(5)=\frac{533}{28}, I⁡(6)=157714I(6)=\frac{1577}{14}, … , I′​(1)=−16I^{\prime}(1)=-\frac{1}{6}, I′​(2)=0I^{\prime}(2)=0, I′​(3)=+160I^{\prime}(3)=+\frac{1}{60}, I′​(4)=+115I^{\prime}(4)=+\frac{1}{15}, I′​(5)=+2584I^{\prime}(5)=+\frac{25}{84}, I′​(6)=+117I^{\prime}(6)=+\frac{11}{7}, …  and K⁡(2)=13K(2)=\frac{1}{3}, K⁡(3)=32K(3)=\frac{3}{2}, K⁡(4)=10915K(4)=\frac{109}{15}, K⁡(5)=2456K(5)=\frac{245}{6}, K⁡(6)=11 15342K(6)=\frac{11\,153}{42}, K⁡(7)=23 68112K(7)=\frac{23\,681}{12}, …3737 37 Values I′​(1)=−16I^{\prime}(1)=-\frac{1}{6}, I′​(2)=0I^{\prime}(2)=0 are found from the integral formula, their definition via the sum with the Stirling numbers of the first kind being valid only for n⩾3n\geqslant 3. Strictly speaking, Binet only found first four coefficients for each of these series and incorrectly calculated some of them (e.g. for I⁡(4)I(4) he took 22760\frac{227}{60} instead of 23260=5815\frac{232}{60}=\frac{58}{15}, for K⁡(5)K(5) he took 2453\frac{245}{3} instead of 2456\frac{245}{6}), but otherwise his method and derivations are correct. Binet also remarked that

I′​(n)n⋅1(z)n=O⁡(1nz+1​ln⁡n),n→∞,\frac{I^{\prime}(n)}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{(z)_{n}}\,=\,O\left(\frac{1}{n^{z+1}\ln n}\right)\,,\qquad n\to\infty\,, (92)

which implies that he knew the first--order approximation for the Cauchy numbers of the second kind as early as 1839.3838 38 Note, however, that Binet stated this result without proof (he wrote Je ne développe pas ici ces résultats, parce que les détails sont un peu longs). In 1923 Niels E. Nørlund [112, pp. 243–244], [151, p. 335] obtained two series of a similar nature for the polygamma functions. In particular, for the Digamma function, he provided following expressions

Ψ⁡(z)=ln⁡z−1z+∑n=1∞C2,nn⋅1(z+1)nΨ⁡(z)=ln⁡z−12​z−∑n=2∞|Gn|⋅(n−1)!(z)n\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle\Psi(z)\,=\,\ln z-\frac{1}{z}+\!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{C_{2,n}}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{(z+1)_{n}}\\[14.22636pt] \displaystyle\Psi(z)\,=\,\ln z-\frac{1}{2z}-\!\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{\big|G_{n}\big|\cdot(n-1)!}{(z)_{n}}\end{array} (93)

A careful inspection of both formulæ reveals that they actually are rewritten versions of the foregoing expansions for Ψ⁡(z)\Psi(z) given by Binet 84 years earlier.3939 39 In order to reduce first Binet’s series to first Nørlund’s series, it suffices to remark that ∑n=2∞(n−1)!(z+1)n=∑n=1∞1⋅2⋯n(z+1)(z+2)⋯(z+n+1)=1z−1z+1\sum\limits_{n=2}^{\infty}\!\frac{(n-1)!}{(z+1)_{n}}=\sum\limits_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{1\cdot 2\cdots n}{(z+1)(z+2)\cdots(z+n+1)}=\frac{1}{\,z\,}-\frac{1}{\,z+1\,} and C2,1=12C_{2,1}=\frac{1}{2}. The equivalence between second Binet’s series and second Nørlund’s series follows from the fact that 12​[K⁡(n)−n​K​(n−1)]=n​C2,n−1−C2,n=|C1,n|≡|Gn|⋅n!\frac{1}{2}\big[K(n)-nK(n-1)\big]=nC_{2,n-1}-C_{2,n}=\big|C_{1,n}\big|\equiv\big|G_{n}\big|\cdot n!\,, where K⁡(1)=0K(1)=0 and n=2,3,4,…n=2,3,4,\ldots One may also notice that Fontana–Masceroni series (12), (47), is a particular case of the latter formula when z=1z=1. In contrast, the former expression at z=1z=1 yields a not particularly well–known series for Euler’s constant

γ= 1−∑n=1∞C2,nn⋅(n+1)!= 1−14−572−132−25114 400−191728−19 0872 540 160−…\gamma\,=\,1-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{C_{2,n}}{\,n\cdot(n+1)!\,}=\,1-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{5}{72}-\frac{1}{32}-\frac{251}{14\,400}-\frac{19}{1728}-\frac{19\,087}{2\,540\,160}-\ldots (94)

which is, in fact, closely related to the above–mentioned Fontana–Masceroni series and may be reduced to the latter by means of the recurrence relation

nC2,n−1−C2,n=|C1,n|≡|Gn|⋅n!,C2,0=1,n=1,2,3,…nC_{2,n-1}-C_{2,n}=\big|C_{1,n}\big|\equiv\big|G_{n}\big|\cdot n!\,,\qquad C_{2,0}=1\,,\quad n=1,2,3,\ldots (95)

Namely, by partial fraction decomposition, (94) becomes

γ= 1−∑n=1∞C2,nn!⋅1n⁡(n+1)= 1−∑n=1∞C2,nn⋅n!+∑n=1∞C2,n(n+1)!== 1−∑n=1∞C2,n−1−|Gn|⋅(n−1)!n!+∑n=1∞C2,n(n+1)!=∑n=1∞|Gn|n\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle\gamma\,=\,1-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{C_{2,n}}{\,n!\,}\cdot\frac{1}{\,n(n+1)\,}\,=\,1-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{C_{2,n}}{\,n\cdot n!\,}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{C_{2,n}}{\,(n+1)!\,}\,=\\[17.07164pt] \displaystyle\phantom{\gamma\,}=\,1-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{C_{2,n-1}-\big|G_{n}\big|\cdot(n-1)!}{\,n!\,}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{C_{2,n}}{\,(n+1)!\,}\,=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\!\frac{\,\big|G_{n}\big|\,}{\,n\,}\end{array}

It is interesting to note that series (94) converges at the same rate as ∑n−2​ln−1​n\sum n^{-2}\ln^{-1}n, while Fontana–Masceroni series (12), (47) converges slightly faster, as ∑n−2​ln−2​n\sum n^{-2}\ln^{-2}n, see (21). It seems also appropriate to note here, that apart from Nørlund, the series expansions equivalent or similar to those derived by Binet in 1839, were also obtained (sometimes simply rediscovered, sometimes generalized) by various contemporaneous writers, see e.g. [35, p. 2052, Eq. (1.17)], [36, p. 11], [107], [167, pp. 4005–4007].
